newsitem.title: DENMARK: OECD says Danish growth strong, warns on prices.
newsitem.headline: OECD says Danish growth strong, warns on prices.

text.p: Higher earnings, lower unemployment and increased property prices are boosting Danish growth but could fuel inflation, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday.

In a biannual report, the Paris-based think tank said Danish growth had in 1996 been largely driven by domestic demand, but it saw exports rising by four percent in 1997 and five percent in 1998 after a slow three percent increase in 1996.
"The combination of lower interest rates and a quickening of export market growth should sustain economic growth over the next two years," it said.
"However, inflation pressures could emerge with higher employment growth and a closing output gap," it added.
The OECD estimated 1996 GDP (gross domestic product) growth at 1.9 percent and saw it rising to 2.9 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998.
A December 10 Danish government forecast put 1996 growth at 2.2 percent, with GDP rising to 2.9 percent in 1997 but slipping again to 2.7 percent in 1998.
The government predicted inflation of 2.3 percent next year and 1998 but the OECD saw 1997 prices rising by 2.5 percent and nearing 3.0 percent the following year.
The OECD report saw Denmark's public sector budget running a deficit in 1997 equal to 0.5 percent of GDP -- about six billion crowns -- and going into balance the following year.
The Danish economy ministry had made identical forecasts but revised them in its December survey to show a two billion crown surplus in 1997 and 4.8 billion surplus in 1998.
The ministry's accompanying commentary said there was no increased danger of economic overheating, but the OECD appeared less sure.
"There is a risk to the forecast from possible faster domestic demand and inflation," it said. Key figures of OECD report (changes in percent, 1980 prices)
